title: Kubernetes Monitoring & Observability
description: Monitor cluster health with metrics, logs, and health probes for production Kubernetes.

data.text: **Observability** is the ability to understand the internal state of a system from its external outputs. In Kubernetes, the three pillars of observability are: **metrics** (numerical data like CPU usage), **logs** (discrete events like error messages), and **traces** (request flows across services). Together, these give you a complete picture of your application's health and behavior.

terms.definition: Numerical measurements collected at regular intervals (e.g., CPU usage, request latency).
Discrete timestamped events emitted by applications and infrastructure.
End-to-end records of a request as it flows through multiple services.
Tells Kubernetes if a container is running; if it fails, Kubernetes restarts the Pod.
Tells Kubernetes if a Pod is ready to serve traffic; if it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints.

data.text: Kubernetes uses **liveness** and **readiness** probes to manage Pod lifecycle. Without them, Kubernetes doesn't know if your application is healthy or ready to serve traffic. A failing liveness probe triggers a container restart, while a failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the Service endpoint list.

data.title: Liveness and readiness probes
data.content: Configure HTTP health checks for an application container.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: myapi:1.0
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5

cards.title: Liveness
cards.description: Determines if the container needs to be restarted.
cons: Can cause restart storms if misconfigured

cards.title: Readiness
cards.description: Determines if the container can accept traffic.
cons: Pod won't get traffic if unhealthy

cards.title: Startup
cards.description: Gives a container more time to start before liveness kicks in.
cons: Only available in newer Kubernetes versions

data.title: Probe best practices
data.text: Always set an initialDelaySeconds that's longer than your app's startup time. Use a lightweight endpoint for probes — don't hit a database or external service.

Kubernetes ships with **Metrics Server** for basic resource metrics (CPU, memory). For production, **Prometheus** is the standard monitoring stack. It scrapes metrics from your applications and the Kubernetes API, stores them in a time-series database, and provides an efficient query language (PromQL).

data.title: Prometheus + Grafana with Helm
data.content: Deploy the standard Kubernetes monitoring stack using the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart.
data.code:
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

helm install k8s-monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring \
  --create-namespace \
  --set grafana.adminPassword='admin123'

data.text: For logs, `kubectl logs` is useful for debugging individual Pods, but production requires centralized logging. The standard stack is **Loki** (log aggregation) + **Promtail** (log shipper) + **Grafana** (visualization), or the **EFK stack** (Elasticsearch, Fluentd, Kibana).

data.title: Checking logs with kubectl
data.content: View and stream logs from your Pods.
data.code:
# View logs from a specific pod
kubectl logs my-app-7d5b8c9c4-xk2v4

# Follow logs in real time
kubectl logs -f my-app-7d5b8c9c4-xk2v4

# View logs from all pods of a deployment
kubectl logs -l app=my-app --all-containers=true

# View previous container logs (e.g., after crash)
kubectl logs --previous my-app-7d5b8c9c4-xk2v4

data.title: Structured logging
data.text: Write logs in JSON format with structured fields (timestamp, level, trace_id). This makes them searchable and correlatable in tools like Loki or Elasticsearch.

data.description: Improve the reliability of a Kubernetes deployment with proper health checks.
steps: Write a Deployment YAML for a simple HTTP app.

data.expectedOutcome: Pods restart automatically on liveness failures and traffic is routed only to ready Pods.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Observability has three pillars: metrics, logs, and traces.
Health probes (liveness, readiness, startup) are essential for self-healing.
Metrics Server gives basic metrics; Prometheus + Grafana gives production-grade monitoring.
Centralized logging (Loki/EFK) replaces scattered kubectl logs.
Structured JSON logs are easier to search and correlate.
data.takeaway: Without observability, you are flying blind in production. Make monitoring a first-class concern.
